newsitem.title: GERMANY: Mercedes A-class model will cost from 30,360 dmk.
newsitem.headline: Mercedes A-class model will cost from 30,360 dmk.

text.p: Mercedes-Benz AG said on Wednesday its new A-class compact car will hit showrooms in October priced at 30,360 marks ($17,600) for the basic, 1.4 litre, 82 horsepower "Classic" version.

Equipped with a more powerful 1.6 litre, 102 horsepower engine the A-class will retail at 32,430 marks, Daimler-Benz AG management board member Dieter Zetsche told reporters in Rastatt, where the car will be built.
From the second quarter of 1998, Mercedes will also offer an A class version with a 90 horsepower turbodiesel engine which will retail at 34,385 marks.
Two further upgraded models, "Elegance" and "Avantgarde," will be priced at about 2,600 marks above the basis version.
The A-class will be presented on May 7 in Frankfurt in a glitzy show on the city's famous Opernplatz, kicking off a touring road show complete with dancers in a six-storey high steel cube.
Zetsche said clients can start ordering cars from May 5 and predicted that by the end of the year orders will be sufficient to cover the entire 1998 production of A-class car.
Mercedes aims to sell 28,000 A class cars this year and 180,000 in 1998.

The car, which rivals the Volkswagen AG's Golf and Audi A3 cars, marks a bid to lure younger customers into the Mercedes brand and help expand Mercedes sales to one million vehicles by the turn of the century.

Mercedes knows very well it must revamp its image to attract buyers for the A-class -- aimed at 30-something singles, two-person households and hip young families -- in a difficult sales environment for the Stuttgart-based group.
The price of just over 30,000 marks is about half the price of other Mercedes cars.
Zetsche said Mercedes was aware of how competitive that segment of the market is and knew were less prepared to accept long waits for delivery.

"That's why we should try to keep delivery times below half a year," Zetsche said. Daimler's Rastatt plant has capacity to build 200,000 cars per year and can expand that by between 10 and 15 percent if necessary.
As part of its sales drive Mercedes will change its sales strategy to appeal more to younger buyers. "We don't want marble palaces that make you afraid to cross the threshhold," Zetsche said.
The company was aiming for open, friendly showrooms and may have to revamp some of them. Mercedes is now starting to train up 6,500 salespeople from all across Europe for the A-class.
Mercedes spent millions of marks for marketing campaigns to build up a potential customer base of more than 300,000 names, of which 140,000 are considered by Mercedes to be "hot prospects."
